The must-sees

12 places Wizzy will tap you for first, each with a story and something to look for.

  1. 01
    Landmark

    Acropolis

    Most of its temples were built in the 5th century BC under Pericles, after the Persians sacked the earlier ones. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1987.

    Look for

    As you climb through the Propylaia gateway, the small Temple of Athena Nike stands on its bastion to your right.

  2. 02
    Museum · 2009

    Acropolis Museum

    Bernard Tschumi designed it, and it opened in 2009. Its top-floor gallery lines up with the Parthenon, showing the original frieze beside casts of the pieces still held in London.

    Look for

    Glass floors at the entrance and in the forecourt look down onto the excavated streets and houses of an ancient Athenian neighbourhood.

  3. 03
    Landmark

    Ancient Agora

    This was the heart of public life, where Socrates walked and talked. Excavations by the American School of Classical Studies began in the 1930s.

    Look for

    On the low hill to the west, the Temple of Hephaestus still has its full ring of columns, one of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere.

  4. 04
    Civic building · 1843

    Hellenic Parliament

    Friedrich von Gärtner designed it as the royal palace for King Otto, finished in 1843. The Greek parliament has met here since the 1930s.

    Look for

    Below the front, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier shows a dying ancient warrior. The Evzones guards, in pleated kilts and pompom shoes, change every hour.

  5. 05
    Viewpoint

    Mount Lycabettus

    The chapel of St George crowns the summit, reached by footpath or a funicular railway. On a clear day the view stretches from the Acropolis to Piraeus and the islands.

    Look for

    The funicular runs in a tunnel inside the rock, so the view comes all at once when you step out near the top.

  6. 06
    Museum

    National Archaeological Museum

    Its treasures include the gold Mask of Agamemnon from Mycenae and the bronze god from Artemision. It also holds the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient geared device for modelling the heavens.

    Look for

    Find the bronze Jockey of Artemision, a small boy on a galloping horse, raised from the same wreck as the bronze god.

  7. 07
    Venue · 161 CE

    Odeon of Herodes Atticus

    Herodes Atticus, a rich Roman-era Athenian, built it in memory of his wife Regilla. Restored in the 1950s, it hosts concerts and plays of the Athens Festival each summer.

    Look for

    The arched stage wall is the original Roman masonry; the gleaming marble seats were relaid in the 1950s restoration.

  8. 08
    Venue

    Panathenaic Stadium

    It stands on the site of an ancient stadium and was rebuilt in marble, with money from Georgios Averoff, for the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. The Olympic flame is handed over to each host city here.

    Look for

    Notice the hairpin bend at the curved end: the track keeps its ancient shape, far too tight for modern racing.

  9. 09
    Landmark · 438 BCE

    Parthenon

    Ictinus and Callicrates designed it, with sculpture overseen by Phidias, and it was dedicated in 438 BC. It was blown apart in 1687 when a Venetian shell hit gunpowder stored inside.

  10. 10
    Neighbourhood

    Plaka

    It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited quarters of the city. Much of what stands today dates from the 19th century, when Athens became the capital of modern Greece.

    Look for

    Climb into Anafiotika, a cluster of whitewashed island houses built by stonemasons from Anafi who came to work on King Otto’s new capital.

  11. 11
    Square

    Syntagma Square

    Its name means Constitution Square, after the 1843 uprising that forced King Otto to grant a constitution. It has been the stage for major celebrations and protests ever since.

    Look for

    Go down into the metro station: glass cases and a cut-away wall show the graves, pipes and roads found while digging it.

  12. 12
    Landmark

    Temple of Olympian Zeus

    Work began in the 6th century BC but it was only finished by the emperor Hadrian around six centuries later. Fifteen columns still stand; a sixteenth lies where a storm blew it down in 1852.

    Look for

    At the corner stands Hadrian’s Arch. The inscription on one side calls this Athens, the city of Theseus; the other calls it the city of Hadrian.
